issues.legal_issue: A charge for recording a change of ownership in municipal assessment records is a tax rather than a fee when its primary purpose is revenue raising and it is not imposed for a special service to the person charged.
material_facts: The municipality required a substantial charge to record transfers or devolution of title in its assessment books.
The recording process served the municipality’s fiscal purpose of identifying persons liable for municipal rates and did not provide a special service or benefit to the transferee.
The charge was calculated by reference to the property’s value for certain forms of transfer, although mutation was part of the municipal taxation process.
The statutory framework placed mutation within the taxation provisions and separately provided for the municipality’s civic services and taxation powers.
issues.conclusion: The impugned mutation charge was a tax, not a fee, because its primary purpose was to augment revenue and it was not consideration for a special service; it therefore fell beyond the authority to prescribe mutation fees.
issues.legal_principle: The substance and primary purpose of an impost, rather than its label, determine whether it is a tax or fee. A fee requires a connection to a service or regulatory activity benefiting the person charged or a group to which that person belongs; a regulatory charge without a connection to the cost or expense of administering the regulation cannot be imposed as a fee. The Court applied sections 29, 30, 170, 183(5) and 602 of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, as amended, and relied on State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd. (2004) 10 SCC 201; Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of U.P. (1990) 1 SCC 109; Commissioner of Central Excise v. Chhata Sugar Co. Ltd. (2004) 3 SCC 466; Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema (AIR 1965 SC 1107); Municipal Corporation, Amritsar v. Senior Superintendent of Post Offices (2004) 3 SCC 92; and Nand Kishwar Bux Roy v. Gopal Bux Rai (AIR 1940 PC 93).

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_mutation_impost: A person challenged a municipal charge imposed for recording a change of ownership in assessment records.
predicates.primary_purpose_is_revenue: The charge was imposed primarily to raise revenue rather than primarily to regulate conduct.
predicates.no_special_service_is_rendered: The municipality recorded the ownership change for its own fiscal administration and did not render a special service to the person charged or the group to which that person belonged.

issues.definition: When a municipal mutation-impost challenge concerns a revenue-raising charge for which no special service is rendered, the impost is a tax rather than a fee.

issues.legal_issue: Differential charges for the same municipal mutation process violate equality when they vary by property value or the cause of the ownership change despite the same work and expense being involved.
material_facts: The municipality charged different rates depending on the property’s value and on whether ownership changed by transfer or succession.
The municipality performed the same examination and record-changing function for the different categories of applicants.
The expenses of recording the mutation did not vary with the property’s value or the cause of the ownership change.
The charge imposed on some categories was disproportionate to the service said to be provided.
issues.conclusion: The differential mutation charges were irrational, arbitrary and discriminatory, and violated Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: A classification must rest on an intelligible differentia and that differentia must have a reasonable nexus with the object of the legislation. Differential treatment is arbitrary where persons receiving the same municipal function, at the same expense, are charged differently by reference to property value or the cause of mutation without a reason for that distinction. The Court applied Article 14 of the Constitution and relied on Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001) 2 SCC 386.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_differential_mutation_charge and same_mutation_work_for_all_categories and mutation_cost_does_not_vary and charge_varies_by_value_or_transfer_cause

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_differential: A person challenged the constitutionality of different charges for recording municipal ownership changes.
predicates.same_mutation_work_for_all_categories: The municipality performed the same mutation process for applicants in the different categories.
predicates.mutation_cost_does_not_vary: The municipality’s expense of carrying out the mutation process did not vary among the categories.
predicates.charge_varies_by_value_or_transfer_cause: The charge differed according to property value or the cause of the ownership change.

issues.definition: Where the same mutation work costs the same across categories but charges vary by property value or transfer cause, the differential charge violates equality.
